issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a male civilian-in-war-zone trauma profile, sexual objectification as a central trigger is not impossible, but in combination with the rest of the profile it lacks support from memory, threat, and appraisal items. The other items consistently describe war-related threat, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory trauma memory rather than sexualized threat, making this trigger hard to integrate into the same trauma presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding as a trigger is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the selected items. No memory, threat, or appraisal items reference water, drowning, environmental disaster, or any related theme. Given the otherwise interpersonal/war-threat profile, this trigger appears disconnected from the formulation.

issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the indexed trauma type. For a civilian in a war zone, water/flooding and alcohol smell are hard to reconcile with the threat, memory, and appraisal items unless there is some specific unreported trauma context linking them. The rest of the profile centers on generalized danger, distrust, flashbacks, and sensory recall, but these two triggers imply a different situational pattern that is not otherwise represented.

The maladaptive strategy set is partly disconnected from the rest of the formulation. Drug use is plausible as a broad coping strategy, but excessive exercise and concealing clothing suggest body-focused avoidance or managing visibility/safety in a specific way that is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items presented. Given the strong Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies and Threat → Maladaptive Strategies links, these strategies should plausibly follow from the reported triggers and threat beliefs, but these two items do not clearly do so.

vignette:
Arjun Mehta was 24 when he came for treatment, a young American diplomat of South Asian background who had returned from a posting in a war zone several months earlier. He lived with his partner in Washington now, wore pressed shirts and dark jackets to work, and still carried himself with the polish expected in his profession. Yet when he tried to speak about what had happened overseas, he often stopped mid-sentence, jaw tight, and said he knew exactly what had occurred but could not find words for it. The memory was not vague. If anything, it was too clear.

During his posting, Arjun had been part of a civilian diplomatic team working in a city where shelling and sudden attacks had become part of ordinary life. The day that stayed with him had begun as a routine movement between buildings. He remembered the sharp brightness of afternoon light, the sound of traffic trying to continue around checkpoints, and then a blast that seemed to split the whole street open. He remembered the force of it in his chest before he understood what he was hearing. He remembered people dropping, screaming, running without direction. Most of all he remembered the smell: burning, dust, and the raw sting of spilled alcohol from shattered bottles near a damaged storefront, a smell that mixed grotesquely with smoke and heat. He could still picture fragments on the pavement with photographic clarity. When he tried to tell the story in session, he would go silent and shake his head, as if language failed at the exact point the memory became most vivid.

In the weeks after, Arjun continued to work, but his sense of the world changed. He had come to believe there was something about him that had made the event happen, as though his presence, his choices that day, or some flaw in him had placed him there at the exact fatal moment. He also felt stripped of the assumptions he had lived by. He said he had lost faith not only in people’s goodness but in life itself, and in anything larger that might once have made suffering feel containable. When colleagues told him he was safe inside secured compounds or, later, safe back in the United States, he could not believe them. Their reassurance sounded naive to him, disconnected from what he knew now.

His days became organized around moments of alarm. A car backfiring in the street or a dropped metal tray in a café could make him suddenly feel as if he were back there, body tensed and mind flooded, as though the explosion were happening again in real time. If he caught the smell of alcohol on someone’s breath at a reception or embassy event, his stomach turned immediately; for an instant he was back on that street with smoke in the air and shattered glass underfoot. Even thinking about the attack could bring back the smell so strongly that he would pull away from conversation and stare into space. Strangers approaching him in ordinary settings felt dangerous. On the Metro, in building lobbies, even crossing a hotel corridor for work, he watched people closing distance and braced himself before they reached him.

Arjun began responding in ways that made sense to him in the moment, even as they narrowed his life. He started wearing loose, concealing clothing off duty, dark layers and jackets that made him feel less visible, less exposed. At the gym he pushed himself compulsively, staying long after exhaustion set in, as if fatigue and muscle pain could drown out the agitation in his body. At other times he used drugs to get distance from what he carried in his head. He did not describe these choices with pride; he described them as the few things that gave him brief relief from feeling emotionally exposed, a state he found almost intolerable. Vulnerability itself had started to feel like a threat.

These habits began to shape his work and his relationship. Diplomacy required receptions, negotiations, and easy contact with unfamiliar people, but Arjun found himself scanning rooms instead of listening, keeping physical distance, and timing exits. The smell of alcohol at official events was especially hard; he would stand near doors, leave early, or avoid attending if he could. His partner noticed how covered up he stayed even in warm weather, how he returned from punishing runs or workouts drained but still restless, how conversations about the posting ended with him frustrated and mute. He had started to think there was no future for him beyond getting through one day and then the next.

What finally brought him in was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of moments he could no longer explain away. At a diplomatic function, a sudden bang from a service cart sent him into a full flashback in front of colleagues. Later that week, when his partner told him gently that he was home and safe, Arjun realized he did not believe a word of it. He came to treatment frightened by how absolute that conviction felt. He said he wanted help because he could not keep living as though every stranger were a threat and every loud sound a return to that street, but what frightened him most was the possibility that this was permanent—that whatever had been damaged in him had left him with no future to return to.
